name: linux_native_text
doc: The smallest baseline for a text stack: an undecorated row, an SGR colour, an underline, and box rules. What to look for: `blue` in the theme's blue with one rule under `underline`, and on the third row the corner and vertical rules meeting at the same height in the middle of their cells. SGR 1 is set with the colour, so a weight change appears only on an arm whose configured family has a bold face.

name: underline_styles
feed:
\e[4:1m4:1 single, gpqy descenders\e[0m

  \e[4:2m4:2 double, gpqy descenders\e[0m

  \e[4:3m4:3 curly, gpqy descenders\e[0m

  \e[4:4m4:4 dotted, gpqy descenders\e[0m

  \e[4:5m4:5 dashed, gpqy descenders\e[0m
doc: The five SGR 4:x underline styles on one screen: one rule, two rules, a wave, dots and dashes, each under the same gpqy run. skip_ink is at its default, so every rule breaks where a descender stem crosses it. A wrong render draws two of the five alike, or runs a rule straight through the descenders.

name: underline_colored
feed:
\e[58:2::255:80:80m\e[4:3m4:3 curl rule, 58 rgb red\e[0m

  \e[58:5:46m\e[4:1m4:1 rule, 58 index 46 green\e[0m

  \e[4:4m4:4 dots in text colour\e[59m\e[0m
doc: SGR 58 sets a rule's colour while SGR 4:x sets its shape: an rgb red curl, a green rule from palette index 46, and dots with no 58 in force, which take the text colour. A wrong render draws the first two rules in the text colour, or carries a colour past the SGR 0 into the row below.

name: box_drawing
doc: Light box-drawing corners, tees and crosses laid out as a two-by-two grid. Every stroke reaches its cell edge, so the rules run unbroken from cell to cell and each junction is a single crossing. A wrong render leaves a gap at a cell boundary, or steps a vertical sideways between rows.

name: shades_blocks
doc: Three shade levels then the full block, the four half blocks, and a run of shades set edge to edge with no separators. The shades must darken in order and every glyph must reach its own cell's edges, so the run tiles without a seam or a gap between cells.

name: block_mosaics
doc: The ten quadrant blocks and two runs of sextants, each row set edge to edge. Every mosaic must fill exactly its own part of the cell and reach the cell's edges, so a row tiles without a seam; a wrong render blanks a code point, shifts a cell, or leaves a light line between cells.

name: octants
doc: A spread of nine octant blocks, then the first twelve in code point order, both rows set edge to edge. Each glyph must light only its own eighths of the cell and reach the cell's edges; a wrong render blanks a code point or lights the wrong eighth, and the row stops tiling with its neighbours.

name: braille_lattice
doc: Braille drawn as the renderer's dot lattice, which is what a plot, a sparkline or a dithered image is made of: two dot columns and four dot rows per cell, spread over the whole cell, so a block of cells addresses one bitmap. Two rows with every dot raised first, which must come out as one even field — the pitch between two dots either side of a cell boundary is the pitch between two dots of one cell, where the face sets 6 pixels inside against 10 across. Then a row of full left columns, whose dots must stay evenly spaced the whole way along; then a bottom dot row above a top dot row, one ordinary gap apart rather than the cell's whole leftover; then a checker at dot resolution, then a ramp. Every dot is one size. The cell advance is fractional, so a dot placed inside each cell's own rounded rect would land on an alternating pitch and would itself alternate 3 and 4 pixels wide.

name: braille_from_the_font
doc: The same braille block taken from the face instead of the lattice, which is what `font.braille_grid = false` asks for. The dot is the same size and the pattern is the same; the pitch is what differs. A face sets braille to be read, so it groups the dots inside the cell and leaves the rest of the advance around them — 6 pixels between two dots of a cell against 10 across the boundary, and 6, 6, 6 down a cell against 18 to the next row — and a run reads as separated cells rather than one grid. That is right for braille read as text and wrong for braille used as a drawing surface, which is the choice the setting exists to give. The pair with braille_lattice is what shows the setting reaching the renderer rather than merely being stored.

name: powerline_seps
doc: Two indexed background runs, 48;5;31 then 48;5;240, abut in one row with white text on both, and the join has to be a straight cell edge with neither background reaching into the other's cell. Despite the case name the feed carries no U+E0Bx separator glyph, so what is drawn here is a plain colour-run boundary.

name: box_diagonal_joins
doc: The Neovim logo and descending and ascending diagonal runs. Stroke width stays continuous at row joins, with no gaps, doubled antialiased edges, or cap protrusions.

name: box_diagonals
doc: The diagonal glyphs singly, as a run of five crossings, and as two stepped runs descending three rows. Each stroke runs corner to corner in its own cell so a stepped run reads as one straight line. A wrong render shifts a stroke's phase inside its cell, which shows as a kink where two cells meet.

name: color_emoji
feed:
emoji clusters: 2 cells
base       😀
skin tone  👍🏽
ZWJ family 👨‍👩‍👧
flag pair  🇯🇵
VS16 heart ❤️
doc: Five kinds of emoji cluster, each labelled: a bare emoji, a skin-tone modifier, a ZWJ family, a regional-indicator flag, and a VS16 heart. Each cluster is one grapheme two cells wide, so all five glyphs start in the same column; a wrong render breaks a cluster into its parts and pushes that row's glyph right. A face with no colour emoji draws only the heart and leaves the other cells blank.

name: linux_color_emoji
doc: Four emoji runs: a bare emoji, an emoji with a skin-tone modifier, a regional-indicator flag pair, and a heart with VS16, each two cells wide. Where the stack has a colour font all four draw in colour, two cells apiece; the bitmap reference family holds only the heart, so its golden shows one grey glyph and three blank pairs. A run that split a pair into two glyphs, or painted an emoji in the text foreground, shows up here.

name: emoji_presentation_forcing
feed:
bar sits after the glyph
  auto  ☺|
  76:1  \e[76:1m☺\e[0m|
  auto  ☕|
  76:2  \e[76:2m☕\e[0m|
doc: SGR 76:1 forces emoji presentation and 76:2 forces text presentation; the bar printed straight after each glyph marks the first column past it. Auto ☺ takes one cell and auto ☕ takes two, and forcing swaps them, so the bar moves one column right under 76:1 and one column left under 76:2. A wrong render leaves both bars of a pair in the same column, or paints the glyph outside its claim.

name: agree_osc133_marks
doc: OSC 133 around three commands: A before each prompt, C before its output, D with the exit code after it. Every prompt row carries a mark in the left margin and a matching tick at the right edge, blue where the command exited zero and red where it did not; the trailing prompt has no mark because nothing has run in it yet. A mark on an output row, or one colour for both exit codes, is wrong.

name: osc133_marks_monaspace
feed: \e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo [gutter mark shares this centre]\r\n\e]133;C\a[gutter mark shares this centre]\r\n\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$
doc: The OSC 133 prompt-mark bracket centres on the face's own `[` ink box rather than on the ascent/descent midpoint, so the gutter bracket and the brackets typed on the same row share one centre line. Its native tier draws Monaspace Neon, whose `[` sits about 7% of an em below that midpoint, where a metrics-centred mark stands a pixel or two high; the case is strict, so that offset cannot pass as tolerance.

name: password_prompt_lock
doc: A shell's own Password: prompt as the pty delivers it, with [security] password_detect at its default: the heuristic settles on the prompt row and the lock badge stands in the cell after the caret. The case is strict, so a badge that moves a whole pixel fails instead of spending the repaint budget. A wrong render leaves the prompt row bare, or puts the badge on another row.

name: password_prompt_lock_grid_face
doc: The same prompt where the frame is the whole surface: Core paints the lock into the overlay stream, so every arm without a view layer of its own draws the same badge. It is a square-cornered arch over a filled body — the software compositor has no corner radius — standing in the cell after the caret, which keeps its own block. A wrong render drops the badge, rounds it, or draws it over the caret instead of beside it.

name: osc133_marks_grid_face
feed: \e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo [both gutters, red = exit 1]\r\n\e]133;C\a[both gutters, red = exit 1]\r\n\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$
doc: The prompt-mark brackets are composited into the padding on both sides of the command row, so an arm that paints its padding around the grid after drawing it still shows them. The row whose command exited 1 carries a red bracket in each gutter; the bare prompt below it never ran a command and carries none. Blank gutters mean the marks were gathered but never drawn.

name: background_opacity
feed: ground alpha 0.6, ink solid\r\n\e[44m blue \e[0m \e[7m inverse \e[0m  both at 0.6\r\n
doc: [appearance] background_opacity = 0.6: the default ground, the margins, an SGR-coloured cell and an inverse cell all carry alpha 0.6, while glyph ink and the block cursor remain opaque. The comparison reads the alpha channel, so a frame blended over an opaque clear still matches on RGB and fails here; a wrong render is an opaque window that only looks darkened or a cursor faded with its background.

name: background_opacity_marks
feed:
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ this command failed
\e]133;C\agutters keep the body's alpha
\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$ running, ok mark
\e]133;C\a
doc: OSC 133 prompt marks over a translucent window: the bracket is solid ink in a colour pre-mixed with the ground in linear light, so the gutter it stands in keeps the body's alpha rather than compositing denser than either. Row one wears the failed mark, row three the ok one, and the middle row has none; a wrong render thickens the surface under a mark or leaves the gutter's alpha different from the body's.

name: background_opacity_marks_reuse
feed: \e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ first prompt\r\n\e]133;C\agutters keep the body's alpha\r\n
doc: The translucent marks under grid reuse. The second frame ends the first command with status 1, so its mark turns to the failed colour, and opens a second prompt; the third echoes one character over the retained grid. A wrong render leaves a stale bracket or an opaque gutter block where the reused margins were not repainted.

name: background_opacity_reuse_plain
feed: $ first prompt, no marks\r\nmargins keep the body's alpha\r\n
doc: Grid reuse over a translucent window with no marks in play: the second frame adds a prompt row, the third one echoed character, and the dirty rows' margins keep the body's alpha on the reused frame. A wrong render darkens or opaques the margin band beside a repainted row.

name: background_opacity_reuse_nocursor
feed: \e[?25l$ first prompt, no cursor\r\nmargins keep the body's alpha\r\n
doc: The same reuse band with the cursor hidden by a DECTCEM reset, which separates the cursor's own drawing from the dirty-row repaint as the writer of the margin band. A wrong render still shows a denser or opaque band beside the repainted rows, now with no cursor to account for it.

name: background_opacity_bare_prompt
feed: \e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ this command failed\r\n\e]133;C\agutters keep the body's alpha\r\n\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$ bare prompt, no output yet
doc: A prompt that has begun (OSC 133 A) but has started no command (no C) over a translucent window: nothing reserves that row's gutters with an opaque background block while the mark is not yet promoted, so they keep the body's alpha. A wrong render paints an opaque or denser block beside the current prompt row.

name: osc133_marks_clear_to_mark
feed:
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo earlier blocks stay
\e]133;C\aearlier blocks stay
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo their marks stay too
\e]133;C\atheir marks stay too
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ the newest block is dropped
\e]133;C\a\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$
doc: --clear-to-mark drops the newest executed command block and slides the prompt up into its place: the two earlier blocks keep their rows and their gutter brackets, and the bare prompt lands on row 4 with no bracket. A wrong boundary leaves the dropped command on screen, or eats an earlier block and its bracket as well.

name: osc133_marks_clear_preserve_input
feed:
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo this row is cleared away
\e]133;C\athis row is cleared away
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo marks clear with the rows
\e]133;C\amarks clear with the rows
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ only the prompt survives
\e]133;C\a\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$
doc: --clear-preserve-input clears every row and every row mark and keeps the current input line, so one bare prompt is left on row 0 with no bracket. A wrong render leaves an earlier command behind, or an orphaned bracket beside the surviving prompt.

name: osc133_marks_scrolled
feed:
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo mark stays with its own row
\e]133;C\amark stays with its own row
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ echo scrolled back two rows
\e]133;C\ascrolled back two rows
\e]133;D;0\a\e]133;A\a$ this block is below the view
\e]133;C\a\e]133;D;1\a\e]133;A\a$
doc: With the view held two rows back, each bracket stays beside the command row it belongs to instead of a fixed viewport row: the two prompts on screen keep their marks and the newest block sits below the view. A mark placed from the visible row rather than the underlying line lands beside the wrong command.

name: hilite_region_1001
feed:
\e[?1001hrow 1 outside the band
1234start col 5, row 2
row 3 full width
row 4 full width
row 5 outside the band\e[1;5;2;2;4T
doc: Mode 1001's hilite region, set by CSI 1;5;2;2;4 T: the highlight starts at column 5 of row 2 and covers rows 3 and 4 to the full width. Rows 1 and 5 and the first four cells of row 2 stay unhighlighted, and every row says which row it is. A band that starts at the wrong column or spills onto row 5 shows against the text that names it.

name: superscript_subscript
doc: SGR 73 raises and shrinks a run, 74 lowers and shrinks it, 75 returns it to the baseline: the first row sets an exponent, a chemical subscript, and a superscript that switches straight to a subscript, and the last row labels the three states in the state it names. A wrong render leaves 73 and 74 on the baseline at full size, or fails to come back to the baseline after 75.

name: ideogram_attrs
feed:
\e[60mAB\e[65m 60 one rule under

  \e[61mAB\e[65m 61 two rules under

  \e[62mAB\e[65m 62 one rule over

  \e[63mAB\e[65m 63 two rules over

  \e[64mAB\e[65m 64 stress dots above

  \e[64mAB\e[0m 0 clears from here on
doc: SGR 60 to 64 in the horizontal reading each name carries: 60 one rule under the character, 61 two, 62 one rule over it, 63 two, 64 stress dots above; 65 turns them off. The last row sends SGR 0 after AB, so AB keeps its dots and only the text following the reset is unmarked. A wrong render gives two rows the same mark, or strips the mark from the last AB.

name: ideogram_stress_takes_the_text_colour
doc: SGR 58 recolours an underline. The stress mark of SGR 64 is emphasis on the character and keeps the text colour, while the SGR 60 ideogram underline is a rule and takes the recolour — which is why the lower row carries a red rule and the upper row's dots do not. Sixteen marked cells rather than two: a dot is a few pixels, and a couple of them can change colour inside the comparator's tolerance.

name: alt_fonts_fraktur
feed:
\e[10m10 primary face\e[0m

  \e[11m11 alt: same as 10\e[0m

  \e[20m20 fraktur borrows italic\e[0m

  \e[20m20 fraktur\e[23m 23 upright\e[0m
doc: SGR 10 selects the primary face, 11 an alternate that falls back to the primary when no face is configured for it, 20 fraktur, which borrows the italic face, and 23 clears fraktur. Row 2 must be identical to row 1 and the second half of row 4 must be upright; a wrong render keeps a slant after 23 or drops a row onto a different face. On a face with no italic all four rows are shape-identical, and the case then pins only that the selections leave the runs intact.

name: decssdt_indicator
feed: \r\nDECSSDT type 1 status line\r\nrow 8: Line, Column, size
doc: CSI 1 $ ~ turns on the type-1 status line, which the terminal draws itself on the bottom row: the cursor's Line and Column and the grid size. Host text stays in rows 1-7 and never reaches row 8. A blank bottom row means the arm never filled the status row.

name: link_kinds_per_kind
feed:
\e]8;;https://example.com\e\http url: solid rule\e]8;;\e\

  \e]8;;file:///etc/hosts\e\file url: dotted rule\e]8;;\e\

  \e]8;;mailto:a@b.com\e\mailto: dashed rule\e]8;;\e\
doc: With link_style_per_kind on, an OSC 8 link's rule follows its scheme: http solid, file:// dotted, mailto: dashed. A wrong render draws the three rules alike, or leaves the rows with no rule at all.

name: link_style_dotted
doc: link_style = 1 draws every OSC 8 link's rule dotted. The key is an index and the renderers take a VT code that numbers its styles differently, so an arm casting one to the other draws a solid rule here; index 0 cannot show that, because it lands on a code the builder's default arm draws like solid.

name: tek_custom_colors
doc: A Tek 4014 vector chain drawn with tek.color_mode set to Custom: the beam is #33ff66 over a #0a0a0a clear, so the outline is green on near-black whatever the text theme is. A wrong render draws it in the theme's own foreground and background, or loses a vector from the chain.

name: large_font_atlas_clamp
doc: Six letters covering caps height, x-height, an ascender dot and descenders, drawn at the size the case's native profile pins. At 96 pt the glyph atlas's 128x128 grid would exceed the GPU texture limit unless the clamp shrinks it, and the shrunk grid must still index each glyph: a wrong render drops the row or draws the wrong letters. On the bitmap reference tier the same row draws at the ordinary cell size, where nothing is clamped.

name: decdhl_banner
doc: ESC #3 and ESC #4 print the same string as the top and bottom halves of one double-height line, ESC #6 prints a double-width line whose bold run keys its own master, and the last row is the same kind of text at 1x for comparison. The halves must meet at the midline into readable letters and the double rows must advance exactly twice the normal row; a wrong render splits at the wrong midline, so the letters shear or squash.

name: zwj_all_emoji
doc: Every RGI ZWJ emoji sequence, 1614 clusters, on one screen that does not scroll. Each cluster is too long for the cell's inline buffer and lives in the cluster pool, so with all of them on screen at once a bounded pool evicts the earliest ids and those cells resolve to another cluster's sequence. A wrong render repeats a neighbour's emoji or blanks cells that had one.

name: settings_font_jetbrains_mono
feed:
one advance: MWil 0123456789
ligature pairs <> != -> == ===
Regular \e[1mBold\e[22m \e[3mItalic\e[0m
box ┌─┬─┐ joins, powerline 
doc: The configured text family resolves and answers for the whole scene: wide and thin letters on one advance, the ligature pairs, the bold and italic members where the family has them, and the box and private-use glyphs. Its pair, settings_font_symbols_nerd_font_mono, puts a symbol family in the same slot. A wrong render falls back to another face for a row, or drops the box or private-use glyphs to the missing-glyph box.

name: settings_font_symbols_nerd_font_mono
feed:
private use, no fallback
E0B0 E0B1 E0B2 E0B3     
E73C E738 E7A8 E795     
E30D E34C E370 E37B     
doc: A symbol family holds the primary slot and answers for twelve private-use codepoints with no system fallback; the hex at the head of each row names the four beside it. The bundled face carries all twelve, so every one draws its symbol and none draws a missing-glyph box. Its pair, settings_font_jetbrains_mono, holds the same slot with a text family.

name: onefetch_language_icons

name: agree_box_primary_font
doc: Box-drawing joins at light, double and heavy weight, plus rounded corners and two dashed rules, on a light theme. What to look for: each rule runs unbroken through its corner, tee and cross, with no gap or step where it crosses a cell boundary and no change of weight along a run. A glyph that came from somewhere other than the route the rest of the family takes lands at a different height and breaks the join.

name: box_partial_font

On the native tier the line glyphs come from a primary face that covers only part of the inventory while the block geometry is always drawn by the renderer, so a disagreement between the two shows as a rule that misses its join or a block that leaves a gap.

name: box_vertical_stretch

name: box_vertical_stretch_line_spacing_10

name: curly_middle_stack
doc: Both curly braces as three pieces, upper hook over middle piece over lower hook, either side of a one-column gap. The middle piece is the brace's own middle rather than the generic extender, and the three pieces meet with no blank row between them; a wrong piece or a wrong vertical placement leaves a step or a gap at a row join.

name: bracket_stacks
doc: Every three-piece stack that has an extension piece: the integral, both parentheses, both square brackets and both braces, hook over extension over hook. The extension keeps the column and the weight of the hook above it, so each stroke runs unbroken through the cell joins and no join row is darker than its neighbours; a piece routed to a different face steps at the seam, and a piece painting past the edge it continues into darkens one row.

name: powerline_seams_fractional

The separator cell carries the left segment's background as its foreground over the right segment's background, so the two colours meet inside the cell with nothing of either left at its edges. A wrong render leaves a hairline of background at a seam, or draws the same separator differently at different columns.

name: powerline_seams_line_spacing_10

The solid separators still span the taller cell, so no band of segment background opens above or below them, while the thin chevrons and half-disc outlines keep the face's own stroke instead of thickening with the cell. A wrong render puts a horizontal stripe of background between the rows, or a separator that grew heavier with the row.

name: powerline_segment_bar

Each separator cell carries the two segment backgrounds it joins at full contrast, so a wrong render shows a notch of background at a snapped cell edge, or an outline whose shape changes with the column it lands on.

name: powerline_segment_bar_line_spacing_10
doc: The same status bar with ten points of extra line spacing. The solid arrows fill the taller cell top to bottom so neither segment background opens a band above or below them, and the thin chevrons keep the face's stroke rather than thickening with the cell. A wrong render cuts a horizontal stripe of background through the bar's outline.

name: specimen_glyph_plate
doc: Plate V: the graphics repertoire. The light, heavy, double and rounded box families with their corners, tees and crosses, mixed-weight junctions, SCS G0 line drawing, scan lines and bracket pieces, block elements, eighths, shades and sextants, then the sixteen Powerline separators and a segment bar running both ways at full contrast. Every figure on the plate tiles by construction, so a seam between cells, a weight drift, or a junction that misses its rail breaks a visible shape.

name: selection_tint
feed:
the tint covers this whole row
and ends at the last letter
this row has no tint
doc: A character-mode selection from the start of the first row through column 26 of the second: the tint covers the first row to its full width, ends on the last letter of the second, and leaves the third alone. The tint is an overlay, and an arm that composites overlays of its own can drop this one and still agree with every other case. A wrong render shows plain rows, or a tint that stops at the first row's text rather than running to the edge.

name: selection_native
feed:
the fill covers this whole row
and ends at the last letter
this row has no fill
doc: The same selection in the default style: the system's selection colour, opaque, behind glyphs that keep their own colour, the way a text view on the same desktop draws one. The fill is the light appearance's (179, 215, 255) under the default Highlight colour because the theme is light, and it runs to the first row's edge and stops on the last letter of the second. A wrong render shows the translucent tint over the text, a fill that hides the glyphs, or the dark appearance's colour under a light theme.

name: selection_tint_doubled_rows
feed:
#6double width row
#3double height
#4double height
plain row under them
doc: A character-mode selection from logical column 2 of a DECDWL row, over a DECDHL pair, to column 6 of a plain row, in the tint style. The spans the tiers carry are logical columns, and a doubled row draws each across two cells, so the tint on the first three rows starts at twice the column and runs to the grid's edge; on the plain row it ends on the seventh cell. A wrong render tints the DECDWL row from its fourth cell or the DECDHL halves at single width, which puts the tint on the glyphs left of the ones selected.

name: selection_double_height_pair
doc: A character-mode selection of logical columns 2 to 5 placed on the bottom half of a DECDHL pair, in the default style. Both halves of the pair show one line of glyphs, so the fill covers the same four doubled columns on both rows — the whole height of `llo ` — and the plain row below is untouched. A wrong render fills only the bottom half, fills the top half at a different width, or fills the bottom half at single-cell pitch.

name: selection_native_unfocused_dark
feed:
the fill covers this whole row
and ends at the last letter
this row has no fill
doc: The default-style selection in a pane without focus, under a dark theme: the fill is the dark appearance's unemphasised grey, (70, 70, 70), which is what a text view draws for a selection in a window that is not key. The appearance follows the theme's background rather than the session's, and the emphasis follows the pane's focus. A wrong render shows the accent colour of a focused selection, the light appearance's grey, or the tint.

name: search_highlight
feed: needle, other match: dim\r\nneedle, focused match: bright\r\n
doc: --search runs a real search over the two rows, so the highlight comes from the terminal's own search state rather than from spans handed in. Correct: the focused match on row 2 sits on a solid bright fill, the other match on row 1 on the dim tier, and the words themselves are unchanged under both. An arm compositing overlays of its own can drop either tier here and still agree with every other case.

name: linux_search_highlight
feed:
this needle is a match
this needle is the current match
doc: A search for `needle` with two matches on screen. The emphasis is baked into the matched cells rather than composited over them, so an arm that draws its own overlays cannot leave it out and still agree: both matches carry a fill over exactly their six cells, and the current one is the brighter fill with the text drawn dark against it. A run that tinted a whole row, or gave both matches the same fill, is wrong.

name: linux_trigger_highlight
feed:
a highlight trigger is installed
so this ERROR row is tinted
and no other row is
doc: Three rows and a `highlight` rule on the word ERROR, installed from [triggers] before the feed: the middle row alone carries the rule's tint, and the outer two stay plain. A wrong render tints nothing, which is what an arm draws when it never installs the configuration's rules, or tints a row the rule did not match.

name: symbol_fallback_absent
feed:
private use, primary face only
Terminal:   Folder:   Git: 
Powerline:    
doc: The same private-use row with both fallbacks pinned to the primary face, so nothing else can supply a glyph: the terminal, folder and git cells stay empty and only the renderer's own powerline separators draw. A wrong render fills those cells anyway, which means a face was consulted after the configuration ruled it out.

name: wide_clusters
feed:
一́ 一́ 一́ 一́ 一́
一 一 一 一 一
あ́ あ́ あ́ あ́ あ́
あ あ あ あ あ
doc: Two-cell bases carrying a combining acute, each marked row above its unmarked twin. A marked cell goes through the wide-cluster path and draws the same base, at the same size and from the same face, with the mark above it; a backend without that path renders the two rows alike, and one drawing the cluster from another face renders the base at a different size.

name: agree_unifont_attributes
doc: SGR 1;31, 4, 9 and 7 on four self-labelled runs, plus a blue run and the cursor on the second row, held byte-identical across every arm because a bitmap face with no hinter and no antialiaser rasterises a code point to the same bytes everywhere. What to look for: the first run red at the family's one weight, a single rule under the second, a single line across the middle of the third's letters, and the fourth with foreground and background exchanged. A strike drawn at the top of the x-height rather than across the middle of it is wrong.

name: agree_unifont_underline_style
doc: The same feed under an [underline] block: offset 6 pushes the rule six points below where the face puts it, and thickness 3.0 draws it three times the face's own rule, so it clears the descenders and lands on the row beneath. The strike takes the thickness multiplier and keeps its height. A backend that never reads the section renders agree_unifont_attributes' picture instead, a thin rule tight under the baseline, and the two goldens stop differing.

name: agree_unifont_boxdash
doc: Solid, dashed and dotted rules at two weights, the same four verticals in alternating columns, and the corner joints that close them, under a line spacing that grows the cell past the em. What to look for: each dash sits on the same line as the solid rule it continues, and the corners close on that line. A dash routed outside the box family's centring rides the text baseline instead and steps off the rule, which the extra spacing is there to expose.

name: agree_unifont_wide
doc: Two-cell glyphs — two ideographs, a kana and a fullwidth Latin letter — from the family Core rasterises itself, drawn twice on the first row so a wrong advance shows as drift between the groups. The narrow letters on the second row are the control: they come from the same family, so a picture where they draw and the wide cells do not is the wide page alone. No box-drawing character is here, because those take the procedural route and would make the case answer two questions.

name: swift_ligature_chunk_seam
doc: A ligature run longer than the 16-cell shaping chunk, so the row is shaped in pieces and each piece is shaped with its neighbours as context. The context glyphs land in the strip's margins, which is also where an outer cell reaching the slot edge looks for its own overhang: a wrong render paints the seam column twice and it reads bolder than the text around it. Both arms shared that rule, so only a recorded image catches it.

name: swift_ligature_chunk_seam_joined
feed: a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a.a\r\nx->y!=z===w<=>v|>u++t--s::r.q.p.o.n.m.l.k\r\nsame run; read != and === at the seam
doc: The chunk-seam run with the broken-equals stylistic set turned off, so on a face that carries them != and === draw their joined forms across the seam. It pins two claims in one golden: the joined forms survive chunking, and the reader's feature spec beats the probe's in the merge fold. A wrong render splits a joined form at the seam, or draws the broken forms.

name: swift_styled_text
doc: The styled-text baseline: SGR 1, 4 and 7 on the first row, a background run and two foreground colours on the second. The last run is SGR 90, and on this theme bright black lands on the same tone as the default text, so it must read like the plain word rather than stand out. A wrong render loses a background run past its padding spaces, or draws the reverse run without swapping.

name: swift_clusters
feed:
decomposed row, precomposed twin: same
é ñ à ô ü ç
é ñ à ô ü ç
two marks on one base: à́ ê̄ o̲̅
doc: A decomposed base-and-mark row over its precomposed twin: the same six letters in NFD and NFC, which have to draw the same. The last row stacks two marks on one base. A wrong render leaves a bare letter above an accented one, or pushes a mark into the next cell.

name: swift_cursor_bar
doc: DECSCUSR 5: the bar cursor draws as an overlay at the left edge of the cell after the text, full cell height. The snapshot holds the blink on, so the bar is in every correct picture; a wrong render draws a block, or an empty cell.

name: swift_cursor_underline
doc: DECSCUSR 3: the underline cursor draws as an overlay along the bottom of the cell after the text, one cell wide. A wrong render draws a block or a bar, or sets the rule at the glyph underline's height instead of the cell's foot.

name: swift_cursor_hollow
doc: An unfocused pane: the block cursor declines its fill and draws as a stroked outline, the one cursor shape focus alone produces. A wrong render fills the block the way a focused pane does, or drops the cursor.

name: swift_cursor_hollow_wide
feed: 一二 unfocused pane, hollow block\r\nascii row below\e[1;1H
doc: An unfocused pane with the block cursor parked by \e[1;1H on the lead cell of a double-width CJK glyph: the outline declines its fill and strokes the two columns the character occupies, the same two the focused block covers in cursor_on_wide_cell. A wrong render strokes one column, ringing the left half of the glyph and leaving the right half bare, or fills the block the way a focused pane does.

name: swift_double_size
feed:
default line attribute
\e#6DECDWL ┌──┐ meets
\e#3DECDHL halves join
\e#4DECDHL halves join
default line attribute
doc: DECDWL on one row and a DECDHL top-and-bottom pair below it, between two rows at the default line attribute. The box rule on the double-width row must meet across the stretched cells, and the two halves — the same characters written twice — must join at the midline with no seam against the single rows. A wrong render breaks the rule, offsets one half against the other, or draws either row at single size.

name: decdwl_width_axis_monaspace
doc: A DECDWL row in a family with a width axis, over a plain row of the same text and a DECDHL pair. Monaspace Neon's wdth axis runs 100 to 125, so the doubled row is drawn from the face at 125, a quarter wider by design, and only the rest of the doubling is a horizontal scale: stems keep their weight and bowls stay round. The DECDHL pair is doubled both ways and keeps the face at its own width. A wrong render stretches the regular letterforms twice as wide, with vertical stems twice the weight of the horizontals, or widens the DECDHL pair.

name: decdwl_width_axis_sf_pro
doc: A DECDWL row in SF Pro, whose wdth axis reaches 150, over a plain row of the same text and a DECDHL pair. SF Pro is proportional, so every row is laid out as proportional runs at the face's own advances: the plain row packs its letters as the typeface sets them, and the DECDWL row sets the same letters at twice their advances, each drawn from the face at 150, whose Expanded letterforms advance about 1.4 times the regular ones, and scaled across by the rest of its own doubling: 1.44 for H, 1.39 for m, 1.54 for r. The Expanded master draws heavier stems, so the doubled row's stems read about 1.8 times the plain row's while the horizontals keep their weight; that is the face's design, not a stretch. The DECDHL pair keeps the face at its own width, its letters at twice their advances. A wrong render stretches the regular letterforms twice as wide, spaces the plain row's letters a digit cell apart, or widens the DECDHL pair. Held on the CoreText stack: SF Pro ships with macOS alone.
