name: settings_cursor_invert_text_enabled
feed:
invert_text, block on v
row with no cursor[1;3H
doc: [cursor] invert_text on, with the block cursor parked on the v of the first row: the glyph is drawn against the block instead of buried by it, so the v stays readable next to the plain v at the line's end. A wrong render fills the cell solid, which is the picture its disabled twin pins.

name: settings_cursor_invert_text_disabled
feed:
invert_text, block on v
row with no cursor[1;3H
doc: [cursor] invert_text off: the block sits behind the v and preserves its foreground colour. With invert_text on, the glyph instead uses the grayscale inverse of the cursor colour. Hiding the glyph or recolouring it with invert_text off violates this contract.

name: settings_cursor_shape_underline
feed:
underline, rule on d
row with no cursor[1;3H
doc: [cursor] shape = underline and no DECSCUSR anywhere in the feed: the cursor parked on the d of the first row draws as the rule along the cell's foot that the preference names, so a configured shape reaches the render on every arm. A wrong render draws a block, which is what an arm draws when it never seeds the preference and its bare model starts on the block.

name: colorblind_deuteranopia
doc: The red and green palette slots as background swatches and as foreground words, under a named theme with colorblind_mode = deuteranopia. The substitution runs inside theme application, so both slots draw as the substituted pair rather than the theme's own red and green. A wrong render shows the theme's plain red and green, which is what an arm draws when it applies the theme without the reader's colour-vision mode.

name: osc66_proportional_grid_face
doc: Each proportional run prints the cell count it claims, and a bar stands in the cell just past it. A tier with a proportional face shapes the run in that face, a tier without sets the text in the grid face one code point per cell, and either way the run occupies exactly the cells it asked for, so the bars land in the same columns on every tier. A run that spilled past its claim, or a face that changed the cells taken, moves a bar.

name: osc66_proportional_layout
doc: Proportional runs laid out against the grid: a bold run, the three alignment keys, one key at two claim widths, two runs whose SGR background covers every cell they claim, and four narrow letters beside four wide ones at the claims a q=1 measurement gives them. Where a tier has a proportional face the run is shaped in it and h moves the text inside the claim (h=1 right, h=2 centred); where it has none the text is set in the grid face from the anchor, so the bars, not the ink, are what must agree between tiers. Every run fits its claim here; a run that does not is osc66_proportional_overflow.

name: osc66_proportional_overflow
feed:
\e[?25l\e]66;p=1:c=3;three cells wide\a| text over c=3
\e]66;p=1:c=4;four cells wide\a| text over c=4
\e]66;p=1:c=5;abcdefghij\a| h=0 cut at c=5
\e]66;p=1:c=5:h=2;abcdefghij\a| h=2 cut at c=5
doc: Every run's text is longer than the cells it claims, so it is cut at its last claimed cell instead of spilling onto its neighbour; the bar marks that cell and the grid text after it names the claim. The last two rows are the same text at the same width under two alignment keys: alignment moves the pen by the slack a fitting run leaves, an overflowing run leaves none, so both keep their head and lose the same tail. A render that let an aligned run keep its tail, or pushed ink past a bar, fails.

name: linux_proportional_layout
doc: OSC 66 proportional runs (Docs/proportional-text.md): a bold run in 16 cells, a label right-aligned and another centred in 18, a run cut at its fourth cell, a run right-aligned in 24 cells (wider than the 16-cell strip slot), and two runs centred in 8 over reverse and coloured backgrounds. The bar after each run stands exactly c cells from the run's first cell whatever the text measured, so a renderer that let the face's own width set the advance moves it. An arm with no proportional face sets the labels in the grid face, one code point per cell, and every bar lands at the text's own length, which is what the unifont and CoreText goldens hold.

name: linux_sized_text
doc: OSC 66 with s=3 on a letter and a full block: an arm that draws sized text sets each run three cells wide and three rows tall, rasterised at that size rather than scaled up from the one-cell raster, which is what the E's stem and the block's edges show. An arm that refuses OSC 66 draws both at one cell, and its golden holds that. A raster that left the enlarged pixel size on the face would draw every cell after the run three times too large.

name: linux_monaspace_text
feed: \e[?25lthe face the config names\r\n\e[1mbold on\e[0m ligatures: -> => != >=\r\n0O1lI confusables |[]{}()
doc: The same three rows drawn in whatever family the tier's config names, so a family that fell through to a substitute shows as different metrics and different letterforms for the same text. The native profile names the bundled variable face by the name its own file declares, `Monaspace Neon Var`, whose wght axis defaults to 200; a config spelling it `Monaspace Neon` matches nothing and fontconfig substitutes another face, which is the failure this case makes visible. The rows hold a run with SGR 1 set, four pairs that ligate in a face that has them, the 0O1lI look-alikes and the bracket set.

name: background_opacity_window_level
doc: The window background painted at half alpha. Translucency also takes the renderer off the grid-cache path, which needs an opaque background, so the frame is composed by the other route and the picture differs from the same scene at full opacity. A render that ignored --bg-opacity would match the opaque scene.

name: tek_glow
doc: DECSET 38 enters Tek 4014, ESC FF clears the page, and one GS vector chain strokes a line low across it, drawn with --tek-glow. Correct: the green beam (#33ff66) over the near-black storage-tube ground (#0a0a0a), the stroke wrapped in an additive halo that fades over several pixels either side; a dropped bloom leaves one hard-edged line of the beam colour. The flag acts only inside Tek mode, so the mode switch is part of the case.

name: tek_custom_background
doc: The same Tek 4014 vector page with --tek-color-mode 1 and --tek-bg #802040 on the command line. Correct: the storage-tube ground behind the beam is that wine colour, overriding the #0a0a0a in the case's tek settings, and the beam stays green (#33ff66) with no bloom. --tek-bg is read only inside the custom colour-mode branch, so a near-black page here means the flag pair did not act.

name: background_image
doc: A background image composited behind a translucent theme background. Destination-over fills only the alpha the theme leaves open, so the case pins --bg-opacity below one: at full opacity the image is invisible by design. The fixture is a gradient with four distinct corners, because a solid colour agrees with any placement.

name: background_image_tile
doc: Tile mode, with the image drawn at 0.6 of its own opacity behind a theme background at 0.85. Repeat addressing pushes the texture coordinates past one, so the window must fill with a lattice of identical gradient squares; a sampler that clamped instead leaves one square in a corner and the rest of the window flat.

name: selection_padded
doc: The selection tint under 40x30 padding, over the words "tinted span" and nothing else. The builder's span overlays carried no origin while the cursor tier did, so an arm compositing Core's overlay stream drew the tint displaced by exactly the padding; at the default padding that read as a small edge residue and was put down to translucent blending. A wrong render puts the tint anywhere but on those eleven cells.

name: trigger_hilite_overlap
feed:
hilite band, rows 1 to 3
the tint covers full rows
last banded row
[?1001h[1;1;1;1;3T
doc: A mode-1001 hilite band asked for over rows 1 to 3 of a five-row screen. The tint covers those three rows edge to edge and stops there, so the row below stays on the theme background; a band off by a row, or one tinting only the cells that carry text, fails.

name: second_frame_overwrite
doc: A second frame that overwrites the retained grid: the base paints two rows, then the frame homes the cursor and rewrites both at the same lengths, so nothing of frame 1 survives. Only the digit differs between the two goldens, so a run that re-snapshotted the first frame shows 'frame 1' where the second golden says 'frame 2'.

name: second_frame_scroll
doc: A second frame that scrolls the retained grid: the base fills all three rows, then the frame feeds one more line from the parked cursor, so the row labelled as leaving goes to scrollback and a new row enters at the bottom. The second golden must start at 'frame 1 row 2' and end with the frame-2 row; a re-snapshot of the first frame still shows the row that should have left.

name: second_frame_identical
feed: frame 2 is empty\r\nthis must not move
doc: The retention control: a second frame fed the empty string. Nothing is written, so re-rendering the retained scene reproduces the base and the idle golden equals the base golden; a retention path that advanced or corrupted state on an empty feed moves these two rows, which the overwrite and scroll cases cannot tell apart from a fresh first frame.

name: box_line_spacing_maximum
doc: A box grid drawn at line_spacing 16 over a 12pt face. The rules keep the stroke weight they carry at default spacing, because the box path keys its stroke to the em rather than to the widened cell; keying it to the cell height draws every rule visibly thicker.

name: framed_encircled_overline
doc: SGR 51, 52 and 53, one per row, then 51 and 53 together on the last. Framed and encircled draw the same four rules around each cell, there being no circle primitive yet, and overline is a rule above the glyph in the underline colour; a dropped decoration leaves its row as plain text.

name: dim_and_conceal
doc: SGR 2 and SGR 8, each beside text at full treatment on the same row. Dim carries the foreground halfway to the background, so the dim word is lighter than the words beside it, and conceal draws no glyph, so its cells stay blank; a render ignoring either prints both rows in full.

name: kitty_image
doc: A Kitty graphics APC (a=T, f=24) transmits a 24x24 raw-RGB payload and displays it at the cursor, under the label the feed prints. Correct: four quadrants at the payload's own 24x24 pixels, which are device pixels at every scale (24x24 device pixels at 1x and at 2x alike, two 12-pixel columns of one row on the 2x native arms and on the Unifont tier's 16-pixel cells) - red top-left, green top-right, blue bottom-left, yellow bottom-right - so a swapped channel order or a flipped placement moves a colour. An empty cell means the APC decode or the blit is gone. The feed ends with a newline, as an emitter's does, so the block cursor waits on the row below the picture rather than over its left column.

name: iterm2_image
doc: An iTerm2 OSC 1337 File= inline image carrying a PNG, which routes to the PNG decode rather than the raw-RGB path kitty_image takes. Correct: the same four quadrants - red top-left, green top-right, blue bottom-left, yellow bottom-right - fitted without stretching inside the requested box. width=24px;height=24px names device pixels, as iTerm2 reads them (its Retina inline images divide N by the backing scale to get points), so the picture is 24x24 device pixels at every scale and on every arm, never rounded to whole cells; it covers two columns of one row on the 2x native arms (12-pixel cells) and on the Unifont tier (16-pixel cells). The block cursor stands right of the picture's last cell, where iTerm2 and kitty leave it, not over its left column. Garbage or an empty cell here while the Kitty golden passes is the PNG decode.

name: sixel_image
doc: A Sixel image (DCS q) of the same four quadrants, four six-pixel bands over a four-entry palette, decoded by a path neither the Kitty nor the iTerm2 case touches. Correct: red top-left, green top-right, blue bottom-left, yellow bottom-right, at the raster's square-pixel aspect without rounding its dimensions to whole cells. Bands that are garbled, shifted, or absent while the other two image goldens pass are the sixel decoder. The feed ends with a newline, so the block cursor waits on the row below the picture rather than over it.

name: dec_special_graphics
doc: A box grid drawn through the DEC Special Graphics charset (ESC ( 0), which maps the letters j to x onto line-drawing pieces, then ESC ( B back to ASCII. The corners, tees, cross, horizontal and vertical come from the charset table rather than from Unicode box code points, and the q and x after the reset print as letters; a wrong table entry draws the wrong piece, and a reset that does not land draws them as a rule and a bar.

name: tab_stops
doc: Horizontal tab from left tokens of one, two and three characters, with the default stop every eight columns. The second field starts at column 9 and the third at column 17 on all three rows, so both right-hand columns line up under each other; an HT advancing a fixed number of cells instead of moving to the next stop leaves them ragged.

name: reverse_with_colors
feed: \e[31;47m red on white \e[0m\r\n\e[7;31;47m white on red \e[0m\r\n\e[7mdefault reversed\e[0m
doc: SGR 7 over an explicit pen: red on white, the same pen with reverse added, then bare reverse over the theme's own colours. The reversed row paints white on red, the swap of the row above it, and the last row inverts the default pair; a reverse swapping the default colours instead of the explicit pen leaves the middle row looking like the first.

name: wide_colored_background
feed: \e[41m一二三\e[0m 6 red\r\n\e[42mAB一CD二\e[0m 8 green\r\n一二三 no fill
doc: A background colour behind double-width glyphs, where the fill has to span both cells of each glyph. Row 1 is three wide glyphs on red, so the red must run six unbroken cells; row 2 mixes narrow and wide on green, so the fill follows the two-cell advance mid-run for eight; row 3 draws the same glyphs with no fill, as the advance control. A fill that covered only a wide glyph's lead cell breaks each run into stripes.

name: background_colour_erase
feed: theme bg, no erase\r\n\e[41m\e[2KEL2 red row\r\n\e[44mblue bg \e[KEL0\e[0m
doc: Background-colour erase: a cell cleared by an erase keeps the pen's colours, so blanked cells paint in the active SGR background rather than the theme default. Row 2 sets red and erases the whole line with EL2, which must read as one unbroken red row across all twenty columns; row 3 sets blue, prints, then erases to the end of the line with EL0, so blue must run on from the last character to the right margin. An erase that painted the theme default leaves both rows on the theme background.

name: scroll_region
doc: DECSTBM confines scrolling to rows 3-5, and five lines are fed into that band, so it scrolls twice and ends holding lines 3, 4 and 5. The two rows above the band say they never scroll, and they must not move. A scroll that ignored the margins pushes them off the top; one that scrolled the wrong rows leaves lines 1 and 2 in the band.

name: 256_colour_palette
doc: The 256-colour palette's colour cube and grey ramp, as Core computes the indices. Row 1 sets backgrounds at five cube indices (16, 46, 196, 226, 21), row 2 is written in cube index 208, which resolves to an orange, and row 3 steps the ramp from 232 to 255. A wrong cube or ramp formula puts another colour in a swatch, or takes row 2 off orange.

name: screen_reverse_decscnm
feed: \e[?5hdark ink, light bg\r\n\e[31mred fg stays red\e[0m\r\n\e[42mgreen bg stays green\e[0m
doc: DECSCNM (\e[?5h) swaps the frame's default foreground and background and leaves explicitly coloured cells alone. Correct: row 1's default text is dark ink on a light ground, the inverse of the untouched frame, while row 2 keeps its red foreground and row 3 its green background against that flipped ground. A reverse that flipped the explicit cells too, or left the default ground unflipped, fails here.

name: decsca_selective_erase
doc: DECSCA guards the cells written under it, and a selective erase leaves them alone. The word 'protected' is written with the guard on, the rest of row 1 and all of row 2 with it off; the cursor is then homed and DECSED erases to the end of the display, so 'protected' is all that survives. An erase that ignored the guard takes it too, and one that never fired leaves the erased words on screen.

name: rectangular_erase
doc: DECERA blanks a rectangle instead of whole lines. Six rows of '#' are erased over rows 2-5 and columns 3-9, so the field keeps a solid row above and below the hole and a flank of hashes on each side of it. A line-wise erase clears whole rows and takes the flanks with it; an off-by-one on either pair of bounds mis-sizes the hole.

name: osc4_palette_recolour
doc: OSC 4 redefines one palette slot, and the cells already written in that slot repaint. Row 1 is written in index 1 and row 2 in index 2, then index 1 is redefined to a blue: row 1 must come out blue, row 2 must stay green. A cell that resolved its colour at write time leaves row 1 red, and a redefinition that hit the wrong slot moves row 2.

name: double_height_coloured
doc: SGR 44;37 on a DECDHL double-height line: \e#3 draws the top half on row 1 and \e#4 the bottom half on row 2, so the two rows read as one line of doubled glyphs. Correct: 'double' in white on an unbroken blue ground, twice as tall and twice as wide as the same word on row 3, the halves meeting at the midline with no seam and no colour break. A path that dropped the pen draws the word in the default ink on no ground.

name: osc10_default_fg_recolour
doc: OSC 10 redefines the default foreground, and the cells already written in it repaint. Row 1 sets no colour and row 2 sets SGR 31, then the default foreground is redefined to an orange: row 1 must come out orange, row 2 must stay red. A cell that copied the default colour when it was written keeps the theme's foreground on row 1; one that took the new colour everywhere moves row 2 too.

name: cursor_on_wide_cell
doc: The focused block cursor parked by \e[1;1H on the lead cell of a double-width CJK glyph. Correct: the block is two columns wide, covering both halves of the wide glyph with the glyph showing through it, while a cell on row 2 is one column. A cursor sized to a single cell width paints only the left half and leaves the right half on the plain ground.

name: erase_line_shapes
doc: The three erase-in-line shapes, one per row, each over the column ruler 12345678 with the cursor at column 5. EL0 erases from the cursor rightwards and leaves 1234; EL1 erases the start through the cursor and leaves 678 in columns 6-8; EL2 clears the row. A wrong direction swaps which digits survive, and an off-by-one at the cursor cell adds or drops the 5.

name: portable_scroll_up_su
doc: SU (CSI Ps S) scrolls the whole display up Ps lines, dropping the top lines and opening blank rows at the bottom. Six numbered lines fill the screen, then CSI 2 S: the golden shows line 3 through line 6 on rows 1-4 and two blank rows below, so the top row names line 3 and the shift reads as two. A wrong count puts a different number on row 1; SD would open the blanks at the top instead.

name: portable_insert_line_il
doc: IL (CSI Ps L) opens Ps blank lines at the cursor row and pushes the rows at and below it down. Four numbered lines are written, the cursor goes to row 2, then CSI 2 L: the golden shows line 1 on row 1, two blank rows, and line 2, line 3, line 4 pushed down to rows 4-6. A render that scrolled the whole screen would move line 1 too; a wrong count opens a gap of another height.

name: portable_delete_line_dl
doc: DL (CSI Ps M) removes Ps lines at the cursor row and pulls the rows below it up, opening blank rows at the bottom. Six numbered lines fill the screen, the cursor goes to row 2, then CSI 2 M: the golden shows line 1 on row 1, line 4, line 5, line 6 on rows 2-4, and two blank rows — line 2 and line 3 gone, with the cursor block sitting on the first cell of line 4. A wrong count deletes a different span; a no-op leaves line 2 on row 2.

name: portable_insert_char_ich
doc: ICH (CSI Ps @) opens Ps blank cells at the cursor column and shifts the rest of the line right, dropping whatever passes the right margin. A column ruler 1-8 fills row 1, the cursor goes to column 3, then CSI 2 @: the golden shows 1 and 2 in place, two blank cells (the cursor block on the first), and the digits 3 4 5 6 moved out to columns 5-8, with 7 and 8 pushed off the edge. A shift the wrong way or a wrong count puts a different digit under column 5.

name: portable_delete_char_dch
doc: DCH (CSI Ps P) removes Ps cells at the cursor column and pulls the rest of the line left, opening blank cells at the right margin. A column ruler 1-8 fills row 1, the cursor goes to column 3, then CSI 2 P: the golden shows 1 and 2 in place, the digit 5 under column 3 with the cursor block on it, 6 7 8 following, and two blank cells at columns 7-8 — digits 3 and 4 gone. A pull the wrong way keeps 3 and 4; a wrong count moves a different digit under the cursor.

name: portable_scroll_down_sd
doc: SD (CSI Ps T) scrolls the whole display down Ps lines, opening blank rows at the top and dropping the bottom lines; the single parameter is what separates it from the five-parameter mouse-highlight form of CSI T. Six numbered lines fill the screen, then CSI 2 T: the golden shows two blank rows, then line 1 through line 4 on rows 3-6, so line 5 and line 6 are gone. A misparse as mouse highlighting moves nothing; SU would open the blanks at the bottom.

name: portable_erase_char_ech
doc: ECH (CSI Ps X) blanks Ps cells at the cursor in place and moves nothing else, which is what separates it from DCH. A column ruler 1-8 fills row 1, the cursor goes to column 3, then CSI 2 X: the golden shows 1 and 2, two blank cells, and 5 6 7 8 still standing at columns 5-8 — where the DCH case pulls the same digits left to columns 3-6. An ECH that shifted would reproduce the DCH golden; one that ran to the end of the line would blank the tail too.

name: portable_dec_fill_rect_decfra
doc: DECFRA (CSI Pch;Pt;Pl;Pb;Pr $ x) fills a rectangle with one repeated character and always takes its corners as a block, whatever DECSACE says. On an empty screen CSI 35;2;3;3;6 $ x fills rows 2-3, columns 3-6 with '#': the golden shows a two-row by four-column block of '#' in blank space, with the cursor still at row 1 column 1 because the fill does not move it. A no-op leaves the screen blank, an off-by-one moves or resizes the block, and a reading-order walk would run row 2 to the right edge.

name: portable_dec_change_attr_rect_deccara
doc: DECCARA (CSI Pt;Pl;Pb;Pr;Ps $ r) turns a rendition on over the cells its corners span, and with DECSACE at its default that extent is a reading-order stream, not a block. Four rows of the column ruler 1-8 fill the screen, then CSI 2;3;3;6;7 $ r sets reverse from row 2 column 3 through row 3 column 6: the golden shows row 2 reversed from the digit 3 to the right edge and row 3 reversed from the left edge to the digit 6, rows 1 and 4 untouched apart from the cursor block on row 4. A block walk would reverse only columns 3-6 on both rows; a whole-screen or empty result moves the reversed cells somewhere else entirely.

name: portable_insert_column_decic
doc: DECIC (CSI Ps ' }) opens Ps blank columns at the cursor column on every row of the scroll region, not only the cursor's row — that is what separates it from ICH. A digit ruler and two letter rulers fill the three rows, the cursor goes to column 3, then CSI 2 ' } inserts two columns: the golden shows a two-column blank band at columns 3-4 down all three rows, 3456 / cdef / CDEF shifted out to columns 5-8, and 78 / gh / GH pushed off the edge. An ICH would leave rows 2 and 3 alone; a wrong count opens a band of another width.

name: portable_delete_column_decdc
doc: DECDC (CSI Ps ' ~) removes Ps columns at the cursor column on every row of the scroll region and pulls the rest left, the mirror of DECIC. A digit ruler and two letter rulers fill the three rows, the cursor goes to column 3, then CSI 2 ' ~ deletes columns 3-4: the golden shows 12 / ab / AB, then 5678 / efgh / EFGH pulled in to columns 3-6, and a two-column blank band at the right of all three rows. A DCH would shorten row 1 only; a pull the wrong way keeps the deleted columns.

name: portable_dec_copy_rect_deccra
doc: DECCRA (CSI Pts;Pls;Pbs;Prs;Pps;Ptd;Pld;Ppd $ v) copies a rectangle to a destination corner and leaves the source standing. Rows 1-2 hold ABCD and abcd, then CSI 1;1;2;4;1;3;1;1 $ v copies rows 1-2, columns 1-4 to row 3, column 1: the golden shows the same two rows twice, upper case above lower case in both copies, so row order and column order survive. A move would blank rows 1-2, a flipped copy would put abcd above ABCD, and a no-op leaves rows 3-4 blank.

name: portable_scrollback_view_offset
doc: Rendering from scrollback: the tool's --view-offset scrolls the drawn viewport up into history, the one path that paints lines the live screen no longer holds. Six numbered lines are written into a four-row screen, so line 1 and line 2 are in history and line 3 to line 6 are live; drawn at offset 2 the golden shows line 1 to line 4, and no cursor, because the cursor's row is below the view. Offset 0 would start at line 3, a dropped history leaves the top two rows blank, and a wrong offset shows a different window.

name: portable_wide_char_line_edge_wrap
doc: A wide character that cannot fit the last column wraps whole rather than splitting. A ruler 1-7 fills columns 1-7 of an eight-column row, leaving one cell; the two-cell '中' does not fit it, so column 8 stays empty and '中' wraps to columns 1-2 of row 2, with 'Z' landing at column 3. The golden shows 1234567 and a blank eighth cell on row 1, 中Z on row 2: a terminal that split the glyph would draw half of it in column 8, and one that packed it into a single cell would put Z at column 2.

name: decssdt_status_line
feed: main display, row one\r\nno status text here\e[2$~\e[1$}status line, last row\e[0$}
doc: DECSSDT 2 (\e[2$~) opens the host-writable status line, DECSASD 1 (\e[1$}) sends the next writes to it, and DECSASD 0 (\e[0$}) hands writing back to the main display. Correct: the two main rows keep their own text and 'status line, last row' appears only on the bottom row, on the arms that draw one; a terminal ignoring DECSASD prints that text into the main grid instead. The unifont picture has no bottom row at all, so on that tier the case pins only that the status write stayed off the main display.

name: osc66_scales_ascending
doc: The kitty text-sizing protocol's scale key from 1 to 5, the same Hg at each: a scale-s block is s cells per character across and s rows down, so the five sit side by side on one anchor row and grow downwards, s=1 being ordinary text. Each block is one glyph at s times the size, the cap height and the descender scaled with it and aligned on the block's own baseline, and every band of a block joins the one above. A wrong render gives a scale the wrong claim, splits a letter at a band seam, or draws a larger scale softer than the smaller ones.

name: osc66_scales_tall
doc: The two largest scales the protocol allows, an H at 6 and a g at 7, the g's descender reaching into its last band. Each is one glyph six or seven rows tall and as many cells wide, its bands joining without a seam. A wrong render clips the block at the grid edge it fits inside, drops a band, or draws the descender outside its block.

name: osc66_width_key
doc: The width key at scale 2. w=0 lets the terminal measure the character, one cell for a letter, so the block is two cells; w=1 names that same cell and draws the same; w=2 and w=3 widen the block to four and six cells with the glyph at the scale's size on its left, the rest of the block its own. The bars mark where each block ends. A wrong render stretches a letter across a wider claim, or gives a block a width its key did not ask for.

name: osc66_width_past_eight_windows
doc: An explicit width wider than the glyph, past eight columns a band: s=3 at w=3 and w=4, and s=7 at w=2. The glyph is drawn once at its scale's size in the block's left columns, the rest of the block stays empty, and the bar after each block stands at its claim. A renderer that counts windows across the block rather than the glyph refuses the windows and draws the glyph soft, or as misregistered slices.

name: osc66_selection_block
doc: A drag from the A to the cell holding the first block's top band. The selection's own row ends at that band, and the block is selected whole: the highlight covers its two columns on both of its rows, as kitty does, while the next block, which the drag does not touch, stays unlit. A wrong render lights only the anchor row of the block, leaving its lower band bare, or lights the second block too. The selection is drawn in Core's tint, so the five arms share one picture: the native style would take the platform's own colour on the macOS arms and none on the others.

name: osc66_selection_block_gap
doc: A drag from the second l of hello, which stands to the right of a block on its row, down to the third row. The row below holds the block's lower band, so the selection touches the block and selects it whole: both of its rows are lit across its two columns, while the cells between the block and the drag's start on the first row stay unlit. A wrong render leaves the block's top band bare, or lights the cells between it and the start. The selection is drawn in Core's tint, so the five arms share one picture: the native style would take the platform's own colour on the macOS arms and none on the others.

name: osc66_selection_block_explicit_width
doc: A drag from the a to the first cell of an explicit-width block, s=2 with w=3. The block claims six columns by two rows around a glyph two cells wide, and it is selected whole: the highlight covers all six columns of both rows, including the claim's empty cells beside the glyph. A wrong render lights only the glyph's columns, or only the top row. The selection is drawn in Core's tint, so the five arms share one picture: the native style would take the platform's own colour on the macOS arms and none on the others.

name: osc66_sheet_pressure
doc: A screen of the largest sized text: the alphabet at s=7, twenty-six blocks of seven bands, every window of every band a slot of its own, which is more windows than a sheet cut for a smaller screen holds. Every block is drawn whole on one path: sharp where the face rasterises at scale, the magnified crop on a bitmap face, and never a block whose upper bands are sharp and lower bands stretched.

name: osc66_fraction_alignment
doc: Kitty's fractional scale. A superscript 2 at s=1 is half a cell high at the cell's top-left. Each A at s=2 claims a two-by-two block and draws at half that, the size of an ordinary A: at the block's top-left with no alignment keys, centred across and down with v=2:h=2, and against the block's bottom-right with v=1:h=1. Hg at s=4 claims two four-by-four blocks and draws each letter two cells high in the middle of its own. A at s=3 claims a three-by-three block and draws one and a half cells high in its middle, from a raster drawn at that size. The bars mark where each block ends. A wrong render draws a letter at its block's full size, or puts the smaller letter somewhere other than where v and h say.

name: osc66_fraction_wide_emoji
doc: A wide CJK character and a colour emoji at s=2 drawn at one half: each claims four cells by two rows and draws at its ordinary two-cell size, at the block's top-left, centred, and against the bottom-right. The bars mark where the pairs end. A wrong render draws either at the block's full size, or leaves the CJK glyph and the emoji in different places within their blocks.

name: osc66_scales_wide_emoji
doc: A wide CJK character and a colour emoji at scales 1, 2 and 3. Each is two cells a scale, so the pair claims four, eight and twelve cells across and one, two and three rows down. The CJK glyph comes from the wide sheet at the block's size and the emoji from the colour sheet, centred in its square. A wrong render draws either at its ordinary size inside a larger claim, crops the emoji at a band, or gives the pair the claim of narrow text.

name: osc66_sized_text
doc: A scale-3 'E' and a scale-3 full block, each taking a three-column, three-row block of cells that must join into one glyph. On the unifont tier each band is cropped out of one master glyph, so a wrong crop stacks three small copies down the block or leaves a single column. On the native tier the block has no atlas glyph and takes the procedural box, which claims all three columns, and the 'E' comes from a master rasterised at the sized point size, so a build that falls back to a magnified 1x crop fails softly. Sizing is gated on Terminal.drawsSizedText, which the snapshot drivers set from --draws-sized-text; without the flag the same feed renders unsized.

name: osc66_sized_wide
doc: A wide character at scale 3: the reference row prints it at its ordinary two cells, the row below claims six columns and three rows. The sized wide glyph comes from the wide sheet's own scale-rasterised master, one two-cell window per claimed slot, so a render that draws it two cells wide, or magnifies the 1x master into a soft block, fails. macOS only: a sized CJK routes to the wide sheet, which the bitmap arm may not bind.

name: osc66_sized_emoji
doc: A colour emoji at scale 3: the reference row prints it at two cells, the row below claims six columns and three rows. A colour glyph's quad is a centred square rather than the cell box, so the band crop lives on the colour path itself; a build that emits the whole master once per band draws three small faces stacked down the block, and one that magnifies the 1x master draws it soft. macOS only: the bitmap arm binds no colour sheet.

name: osc66_sized_double
doc: OSC 66 sizing on a row already doubled by DECDWL. A scale-3 block doubles with its row the way every glyph on it does: the T is six cells wide and three tall, drawn from the width-widened face rather than stretched, as sharp as CoreText's own draw at that size. It stands where its column lies on the doubled row, after the doubled ab, and every band below starts there too, so the stem stands under the middle of the crossbar. The doubled cd follows at the row's pitch, past the six cells the block claims. A wrong render draws the T three cells wide, stretches a three-cell raster to six, places it or its lower bands at the undoubled column, leaves the stem under the left half of the crossbar, or leaves part of the claim unpainted.

name: osc66_sized_double_monaspace
doc: A scale-3 H on a DECDWL row in a family with a width axis, between ab and cd. The block doubles with the row: three rows tall and three doubled cells, six columns, across. Its glyph is drawn from Monaspace Neon at wdth 125 and scaled across by only what the axis left, so its stems keep the weight of the doubled ab beside it. A wrong render keeps the block at its own three columns, stretches the regular H twice as wide with stems twice the weight of its bar, or puts the block over ab or cd.

name: osc66_proportional_double_sf_pro
doc: A proportional run in SF Pro on a DECDWL row, above the same run on a plain row. The doubled run starts at its doubled column, after DWL:, and spans its twelve cells doubled, twenty-four columns; it is drawn from SF Pro at wdth 150, its expanded letterforms, scaled across by only what the axis left. The doubled row holds twenty cells, half the forty columns, and DWL: with the claim leave three, so ' af' ends it and 'ter' wraps to the second row at single width; the plain row follows on the third, and its run keeps its own width. A wrong render keeps the doubled run at its plain width, stretches the regular letterforms twice as wide, draws it over DWL:, or puts the plain row second with no 'ter' before it. Held on the CoreText stack: SF Pro ships with macOS alone.

name: osc66_proportional_double
doc: A proportional run on a row doubled by DECDWL. The run doubles with its row, as the row's own text does: it starts at its doubled column, after the doubled DWL:, and spans its twelve cells doubled, twenty-four columns, with the doubled text after it at the row's pitch past them. This face has no width axis, so its letterforms are drawn twice as wide. The doubled row holds twenty cells, half the forty columns (DEC STD 070 5.6.1: DECDWL halves the length of the active line), and DWL: with the twelve-cell claim leave three of them, so the doubled text after the run is ' af' and 'ter' wraps to the second row at single width. A wrong render keeps the run at its plain width with the rest of the doubled claim empty, draws it over the colon, leaves part of the claim unpainted, or shows no 'ter' at all, written past the doubled row's end into cells it never displays.

name: osc66_decswl_s2
doc: The single-width control for the line-size matrix at scale 2. ESC #6 doubles the row and ESC #5 returns it to single width before anything is written, so ab, a scale-2 H and cd sit at the ordinary pitch: the H is two cells by two rows, on the anchor row after ab, with cd straight after its two columns and its lower band joining the upper one on the row below. A wrong render leaves the row doubled because ESC #5 was ignored, doubles the block for a row attribute the row no longer holds, or splits the H at its band seam.

name: osc66_decswl_s3
doc: The single-width control for the line-size matrix at scale 3. ESC #6 doubles the row and ESC #5 returns it to single width before anything is written, so ab, a scale-3 H and cd sit at the ordinary pitch: the H is three cells by three rows, on the anchor row after ab, with cd straight after its three columns and its two lower bands joining the first. A wrong render leaves the row doubled because ESC #5 was ignored, doubles the block for a row attribute the row no longer holds, or splits the H at a band seam.

name: osc66_decswl_proportional
doc: The single-width control for osc66_proportional_double: a twelve-cell proportional run on a row that ESC #6 doubles and ESC #5 returns to single width before anything is written. The run starts after SWL: at its ordinary column and spans twelve columns at the face's own width, and after follows at the next column. A wrong render doubles the run or the row's text because ESC #5 was ignored, or draws the run over SWL: or after.

name: osc66_decdwl_s2
doc: A scale-2 H on a DECDWL row between ab and cd, the scale-2 point of the row beside osc66_sized_double at scale 3. The block doubles with its row: two rows tall and two doubled cells, four columns, across, after the doubled ab, its lower band on the plain row below at the anchor's doubled column so the stems run straight through the seam. The doubled cd follows at the row's pitch. This face has no width axis, so the glyph is drawn twice as wide as it is tall. A wrong render keeps the block at its own two columns, draws the lower band at the plain row's width so the H's feet are half the width of its body, or puts the block over ab or cd.

name: osc66_decdhl_s2
doc: A scale-2 H on a DECDHL pair. ESC #3 writes ab, the block and cd on the top half; ESC #4 writes ab and cd on the bottom half and steps over the block's lower band. The block keeps its own height, the pair's two rows, and doubles across with the row, four columns, so it reads as one H as tall as the doubled ab beside it and twice as wide as a scale-2 letter, its band seam on the pair's row boundary. ab and cd are each the two halves of one doubled glyph, joined at the midline. A wrong render halves the block a second time, so each half shows a squashed slice of the H, draws a whole H on each half, keeps the block at two columns, or loses the lower band when ESC #4 marks its row.

name: osc66_decdhl_s3
doc: A scale-3 H on a DECDHL pair, its third band on the plain row below. The block is three rows tall and doubles across with its anchor row, six columns; the band on the plain row takes its anchor's width, so it stands at the doubled column under the two above it rather than over the storage the plain row reserves at its own pitch. ab and cd join across the pair's midline. A wrong render draws the last band at the plain row's width, so the H's feet are half the width of its body and stand to the left, halves the block a second time on each half of the pair, or drops a band.

name: osc66_decdhl_proportional
doc: A twelve-cell proportional run on a DECDHL pair, under the same run on a plain row. ESC #3 and ESC #4 each write DHL:, the run and after, as a pair holds its text. The run doubles both ways with the pair: it starts at its anchor's doubled column, spans twenty-four columns, and reads as one line of text as tall as the doubled DHL: and after beside it, its letters drawn at twice the face's size rather than stretched, the top half on the ESC #3 row and the bottom half on the ESC #4 row, joined at the pair's midline where the doubled DHL: joins. A wrong render draws the run at the plain row's size on each half, so two small copies stand one above the other, doubles it across only, so each half shows a whole flattened copy, or shows the same half on both rows.

name: osc66_scaled_proportional
doc: A six-cell proportional run of Hello at OSC 66 scale 1, 2 and 3, with the plain s=2 block of the same text between the first two. At a scale the run is a block: s rows tall and each of its six cells s columns wide, so the bar after it stands 6s columns past the label on its top row and the rows below hold its lower bands. The run is one picture s times the size standing on its top row, its letters laid out as at scale 1, each band row showing the part of the picture inside it, joined where the rows meet. A wrong render draws the run at its own size on every band row, so s small copies stand one above the other, or shows the same band twice.

name: monaspace_prose_page
feed:
A page of prose, set in a face that heals each letter for the ones beside
it. The run walk cuts a row of text like this one into chunks of at most
sixteen cells, and steps a chunk back to a space so that no cut lands inside
a cluster, so one row asks the sheet for a handful of strips and a whole
page asks it for a hundred or more. Every cell that a strip covers then
draws its own slice of it, cut at the cell edge and clamped to the ink the
strip was measured to hold, so a cell whose measured ink is empty draws
nothing at all. For a space that is the right answer. For a letter it is a
hole, and a hole in the middle of a word is what this page is here to show.
Read the rows for gaps: no word may have a blank cell inside it, and no
letter may be drawn in two places at once.
The seams matter as much as the cells do. Where one chunk ends and the next
begins, each of them is shaped with the cells beside it as context, and the
strip each one draws is held back to the ink it owns. A chunk that reached
past its own text would paint its neighbour a second time, and that joint
would read heavier than the text around it, so a bold seam in the middle of
a line is a fault of the same kind as a hole.
Scale is the point of the page. A screen of code sends a few runs down this
path, while a screen of prose sends a strip for every few words of every
row, which is the load the sheet and its budget were sized for. The same
short words come back row after row, and each time one of them must draw
from the strip the sheet already holds rather than from a fresh one cut
beside it. A sheet that lost track of what it held would cut a copy for
every repeat and run out of room before the page ended.
A healed letter takes its form from the letters beside it, and a space
counts as one of them, so the same word can shape one way in the middle of a
line and another way at the end of one. Nothing here needs to be read for
its story. The page is here to fill a screen with the plain shape of prose,
short words with one space between them, and rows enough that a single lost
cell has somewhere to hide.
doc: A full screen of prose under a healing face, which is the population the strip path is sized for: a row of short words is cut into chunks of at most sixteen cells stepped back to spaces, and every covered cell draws its own measured slice of its chunk's strip. A cell whose measured ink reads empty draws nothing, so a lost cell shows as a hole inside a word, and a chunk that reaches past its own text shows as a seam heavier than the text around it.

name: monaspace_seam_slashes
feed: \x1b[?25l\x1b[2;1Hlet strip = rowcells.slice;   /// cap falls mid word, steps back to a space\x1b[3;1H                              /// cap falls in the token, a space saves it\x1b[4;1Haletterrunthatoverrunsthechunk/// letters to slashes, a class change saves it\x1b[5;1H==============/// same class both sides, so the cut stays hard\x1b[6;1H/// at the row start, and path/to/file between letters
doc: A three-cell `///` cluster placed at the sixteen-cell chunk cap four ways, on a face that shapes it as one image whose carrier reaches back past the strip slot's margin, so a seam through it loses its first cell. Rows 2-4 are the rescues the walk has: the cap falls mid-word and steps back to a space, falls inside the token with a space before it, and falls inside the token after a change of operator class. Row 5 is the residual — both sides of the cap are the same class, so the cut stays hard — and row 6 puts the token at the row start and inside a path.

doc: The profile asks for weight 400 with the axis wght=700, and the face is the variable build, so the axis carries the weight and the named weight never runs. On a tier whose face has that axis, all three rows draw heavy — including the two that set no SGR — and every run keeps the columns the regular face gives it. name: agree_cursor_in_last_column
doc: Three probes for the last column of a 20-column grid: 23 letters fix the wrap point, 20 fill a row exactly, and 19 leave the captured cursor parked in the final cell rather than past it. A surface one column narrower than it was asked for moves the wrap, shortens the full row and drops the cursor a column, so it fails all three; a case holding only the cursor would still pass, since a narrow grid has a last column to draw in too.

name: dentistry_elbows_and_scan_line
doc: The three dentistry symbols are East_Asian_Width Neutral, so each takes one cell and the word after it starts in column 2 on all three rows. A terminal that widens them to two cells slides that word to column 3 and corrupts the input of the programs inside it, which is why an earlier widening was reverted. A shape-only golden misses the slide; the starting column catches it.
